newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK shares surge to record close, Tokyo ends higher.
newsitem.headline: HK shares surge to record close, Tokyo ends higher.

text.p: Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index scored an all-time closing high on Thursday as investors snatched up stocks which were left behind in Wednesday's record-breaking rally.
The Hang Seng index soared above the 14,000 point-level for the first time, hitting a record high of 14,004.93 before closing on a gain of 64.03 points at 13,830.68.
"I think there are a lot of momentum players around and a lot of people were caught short of the sharp break-out yesterday," said James Osborn, sales director at ING Barings.
The Hang Seng climbed 472.78 points on Wednesday, as property and banking stocks surged. Utilities and conglomerates played catch up on Thursday.
Elsewhere in Asia, markets were mixed.

Tokyo stocks ended slightly higher after swinging between positive and negative zones. The Nikkei 225 average finished up 51.21 points, or 0.28 percent, at 18,144.34, after fluctuating between 17,970.85 and 18,317.63 points.
"It was a tug of war between bullish and bearish sectors, as the rebound earlier this week was feeble," said Kenichi Sagami, general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
The Nikkei plunged more than 2,000 points last week, sparking fears of an economic crisis, before staging a mild recovery earlier this week.
Shares in some blue-chip counters continued to firm, but overall gains were limited by the financial sector.
Shares in Singapore ended flat, with retail interest focused on small-cap stocks and institutions buying selected blue chips. Foreign funds were mostly lured to the Hong Kong bourse, dealers said.

"The focus is on regional funds, not so much the Singapore dollar stocks," said a dealer. The Straits Times Industrials Index ended 0.79 of a point down at 2,220.36 after trading within a narrow 10-point range.

The Australian share market ended slightly weaker and narrowly mixed, with a firmer resources sector failing to overcome a Dow-weakened industrials group. The All Ordinaries index lost just 1.9 points to 2,436.3 as the market spent the day meandering within a five-point range.

"It's been a pretty good performance to be only down a couple of points with the gold price so weak and Wall Street down," said Steve Mayne, dealer at Brisbane-based brokerage, Nevitts Ltd, adding that the market looked comfortable with its recent higher levels.
The Dow Jones index ended 35.41 points lower at 6,726.88 on Wednesday, after a four-session streak of record closes.
Stocks in Seoul closed sharply higher after recouping earlier losses caused by profit-taking, brokers said. They said sentiment improved as fears of all-out strikes faded.
Buying was buoyed by hopes that foreign investors would shift their attention to Asia because of speculation over an imminent fall on Wall Street, brokers said.
The composite index ended at a provisional 711.86, up 1.73 percent or 12.10 points from Wednesday.

"Buying was across the board as investors were confident the rally would continue a little longer," said Park Sang-woon of Seoul Securities. South Korea has been hit by wildcat strikes since a controversial labour law was passed on December 26.
In Thailand, persistent worries about banks' and finance firms' fourth-quarter earnings triggered selling among local investors, pushing the volatile index down in thin trade.
The SET index dropped 6.34 points to 822.57 on 3.8 billion baht turnover. The SET-50 index retreated 0.57 of a point to 61.32.

Crude oil futures clawed back some early losses in Singapore. February Brent was last traded at $23.60 per barrel, down 24 cents from London's Wednesday close. March attracted the most volume and was last traded 32 cents down at $23.33.
Hong Kong gold ended at US$354.00/50 an ounce against New York's US$352.25/75 close on Wednesday.
The dollar was steady against the mark and yen in Europe. At 1045 GMT, the dollar was at 116.90/95 yen and 1.5894/99 marks.
